You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

=== EXTRACTED CLINICAL ENTITIES — YOU MUST RETAIN ALL OF THESE ===
Patient: male | Age: None
Primary Diagnosis: Sensitive Pulmonary Tuberculosis
  Secondary: Spontaneous pneumothorax on the right
  Secondary: Lung collapse
  Secondary: Bleeding in tuberculous caverns
  Secondary: Surgical wound infection by multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
  Secondary: Hypovolemic shock secondary to surgical wound bleeding
  Secondary: Cardiopulmonary arrest in asystole secondary to hypoxia
Symptoms at admission: Persistent dry cough for 4 weeks without expectoration; Night sweats; Unmeasured fever starting 3 days prior; Dyspnea (shortness of breath); Sudden pain in right hemithorax radiating to right cervical region starting 1 day prior; Weight loss of approximately 8 kg over 1 month
Anomalies/Findings:
  [BORDERLINE] Pallor (pale 1/4+) = 1/4+
  [CRITICAL] Abolished vesicular breath sounds in right hemithorax with asymmetry of expansion = Abolished breath sounds (normal: Normal bilateral vesicular breath sounds)
  [CRITICAL] Sputum Bacilloscopy (Ziehl-Neelsen) = Positive: 10 to 99 BAAR in 100 fields (normal: Negative)
  [NORMAL] Procalcitonin = 0.09 ng/mL (normal: < 0.10 ng/mL)
  [CRITICAL] Hypovolemic shock due to bleeding
  [CRITICAL] Cardiopulmonary arrest in asystole for 4 minutes = 4 minutes asystole (normal: Normal cardiac rhythm)
Procedures performed:
  • Right chest drainage (chest tube placement) on 03/02/2020
  • Pleurostomy on 03/03/2020
  • Closure of pleurostomy and pleural drainage with Heimlich valve on 10/03/2020
  • Removal of Heimlich valve and keeping drain open for ostomy on 27/03/2020
  • New pleurotomy on 31/03/2020
  • Emergency exploratory thoracotomy and cavity packing with compresses on 07/04/2020
  • Right pneumonectomy by lateral thoracotomy and tracheostomy on 11/04/2020
  • Removal of chest drain and tracheostomy tube on 06/06/2020
Medications:
  • Rifampin and Isoniazid (RI) —  | Dosage: Provided 2 months prescription, ongoing treatment
  • Oral iron supplement —  | Dosage: Ongoing oral replacement
  • Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol (RIPE) —  | Dosage: Started 07/02/2020, switched to RI 07/04/2020
  • Vancomycin —  | Dosage: Suspended on 02/04/2020
  • Meropenem —  | Dosage: Suspended on 02/04/2020
  • Amikacin —  | Dosage: Suspended on 02/04/2020
Warning signs to mention:
  ⚠ Sudden difficulty in breathing or shortness of breath
  ⚠ New or worsening chest pain
  ⚠ Coughing up blood or bleeding from surgical wound
  ⚠ High fever or chills
  ⚠ Dizziness, lightheadedness, or sudden weakness
Follow-up appointment: Follow-up appointment scheduled at Infectious Diseases clinic
Follow-up appointment: Follow-up appointment scheduled with the Thoracic Surgery team
Ongoing treatment: Continue oral anti-TB therapy with RI (Rifampin and Isoniazid) for 2 months
Ongoing treatment: Continue oral iron replacement
Ongoing treatment: Carry out follow-up blood and imaging tests
Hospital stay duration: 3 months, 6 days, 7 hours
Outcome: alive
=================================================================
CRITICAL RETENTION RULE: Every entity, value, measurement, date, medication name, finding, and recommendation listed above MUST appear in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. For any measurement (e.g. BP, blood sugar, heart rate, lab values), briefly state what the normal range is and whether the patient's value was within it.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (a machine that cleaned the blood when the kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.
13. CRITICAL — ENTITY RETENTION: Every diagnosis, medication name, procedure, anomaly value, lab result, date, and follow-up instruction listed in the extracted entities block above MUST be explicitly mentioned in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

output_text:
When you were admitted to the hospital on 03/02/2020, you had been experiencing a persistent dry cough for 4 weeks without expectoration (meaning you weren't coughing up phlegm). You also had night sweats, and an unmeasured fever that started 3 days before admission. You were feeling dyspnea (shortness of breath), and for 1 day, you had sudden pain in your right chest area (right hemithorax) that spread to your right neck region (right cervical region). You had also lost approximately 8 kg of weight over 1 month. The doctors noted that you looked a bit pale (pallor 1/4+). When they listened to your chest, they found that the normal breathing sounds (vesicular breath sounds) were completely absent (abolished) in your right chest, and your chest expansion was uneven (asymmetry of expansion). Your heart rate was 85 beats per minute, which is normal (a normal heart rate is usually between 60 and 100 beats per minute), and your heart sounds were normal. Your oxygen saturation was 98%, which is also normal. Your abdomen was flat and soft, and your extremities (arms and legs) showed no swelling or signs of blood clots. Your surgical wound was in good condition and dry, with sutures (stitches) in place and no opening up.

Tests confirmed that you had Sensitive Pulmonary Tuberculosis (TB in your lungs that responds to standard medicines). A sputum Bacilloscopy (Ziehl-Neelsen test), which checks for TB bacteria in your cough sample, was positive, showing 10 to 99 BAAR (TB bacteria) in 100 observed fields, which is not normal. You also developed a spontaneous pneumothorax (where air leaked into the space between your lung and chest wall, causing your lung to collapse) on your right side, which led to a lung collapse.

To treat these issues, a right chest drainage (a tube was put into your chest to remove air/fluid) was done on 03/02/2020. Then, a pleurostomy (a surgical opening into the chest cavity) was performed on 03/03/2020. On 10/03/2020, the pleurostomy was closed, and a pleural drainage with a Heimlich valve (a special one-way valve to let air out but not in) was put in place. The Heimlich valve was removed on 27/03/2020, and the drain was kept open for the ostomy (opening). A new pleurotomy (another surgical opening into the chest) was done on 31/03/2020.

Later, you experienced bleeding in tuberculous caverns (bleeding from cavities formed by TB in your lung). This led to hypovolemic shock (a severe drop in blood pressure due to significant blood loss from the surgical wound). Because of this bleeding, an emergency exploratory thoracotomy (an urgent surgery to open your chest and look inside) was performed on 07/04/2020, and the cavity was packed with compresses (gauze pads to stop the bleeding). On 11/04/2020, you underwent a right pneumonectomy (surgical removal of your entire right lung) through a lateral thoracotomy (an incision on the side of your chest), and a tracheostomy (a surgical opening in your windpipe to help you breathe) was also performed. The chest drain and tracheostomy tube were removed on 06/06/2020.

You also developed a surgical wound infection caused by a type of bacteria called multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (meaning it was a tough infection to treat as many common antibiotics wouldn't work). You were given antibiotics like Vancomycin, Meropenem, and Amikacin for this. These antibiotics were stopped (suspended) on 02/04/2020 after your condition improved and your Procalcitonin level (a blood test marker for infection) was 0.09 ng/mL, which is normal (a normal Procalcitonin level is less than 0.10 ng/mL
